architecture.fell_back_and_why: The plugin subagents named in references/team.md (ehs-web-api, ehs-ai-safety, ehs-infra-cloud, ehs-local-app, ehs-supply-chain, ehs-privacy-abuse, ehs-verifier) are NOT registered in this harness - the available agent types contain no ehs-* entry. I therefore used team.md's documented fallback path: every lane ran as a `general-purpose` subagent whose prompt carried, explicitly, the role file path, the pack paths for that role, the corpus root to substitute for ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, the mode, the target language, the assigned paths, the full safety contract, the return format, the `searched` requirement verbatim and the severity instruction verbatim. This is a documented degradation, not an improvised one: tool access is requested in the prompt rather than enforced by the harness, so the read-only guarantee for the eight audit lanes rests on instruction-following rather than on structure. I verified the tree was unmodified after the run. Dispatch was capped at four sub-agents in flight and collected wave by wave: wave 1 = permit-portal-api, catalog-grpc-store, docwise-assist, edge-fleet-nomad; wave 2 = ledger-reconcile-flows, sitewatch-desktop, supply-chain, privacy-abuse; wave 3 = the two blind verifiers. ALL TEN LANES RETURNED; no lane was declared undone and no lane's findings were written by the lead on its behalf. Independently of the specialists, I read all 57 files of the target myself before and during the waves, and ran the corpus's four helper tools (path_coverage.py, writer_parity.py, default_resolver.py, log_escaper.py) over the whole tree, so every lane had a lead-side reading available to fall back on had it stalled.

findings.title: The /internal admin route group is mounted with no authentication and no rate limiting
findings.class: CWE-306 Missing Authentication for Critical Function / OWASP API5:2023
findings.evidence: routes.swift:35-38 builds the api/v1 group as .grouped(RateLimitMiddleware(...)).grouped(BearerAuthMiddleware()); routes.swift:45 builds the internal group as app.grouped("internal") with no middleware at all. AdminController contains zero req.auth.require calls, against nine in the other two controllers.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller reaching the port can approve/refuse/withdraw any permit and write arbitrary reviewerEmail and internalReviewNotes (a statutory decision, forged, with no audit record anywhere in the app), export any tenant's full permit register as CSV, insert arbitrary attachment index rows, and read session counts. exportAll also builds the whole CSV in memory over an unpaginated result set on the same unauthenticated route.
findings.recommendation: Mount the group behind BearerAuthMiddleware and the rate limiter. That is necessary and not sufficient: the tenant and role defects in the same controller survive it. Add an audit record on approve naming the authenticated staff id.

triage.reason: The only auth middleware in the tree is BearerAuthMiddleware, registered once at routes.swift:38. configure.swift:52-65 registers CORS, ErrorMiddleware and FileMiddleware globally; none authenticates.
Registration at routes.swift:45-46 is unconditional: no environment flag, no #if DEBUG, one Application and one route tree.
The claimed boundary is 'the council LAN' (routes.swift:43-44). A LAN is not a single principal, and exportAll takes an arbitrary tenant UUID, so the second principal is another council's data.
A network control could restrict reachability, but no deployment manifest, gateway config or network policy exists in scope. Absence of that artifact is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every mount point in the tree and joined it against every req.auth.require call site; AdminController appears four times in the first list and zero times in the second.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in the repository narrows it. The prose claim of LAN-only reachability is an external control with no artifact.

searched.for: a globally registered authenticator that would cover /internal without appearing at the mount point
searched.found: three middlewares - CORS, ErrorMiddleware, FileMiddleware. None authenticates.

searched.for: an in-handler auth check, role guard or tenant comparison
searched.found: nothing - no auth.require, no role test, no tenant comparison in any of the four handlers

searched.for: a second listener or bind address that would put /internal on a different interface
searched.found: one Application, one server configuration, one route tree - the segmentation claim is not implemented at the application layer

findings.title: Permit listing cache key omits the tenant, so one council's records are served to another
findings.class: CWE-524 Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information / OWASP API8:2023
findings.evidence: cacheKey = "permits:list:\(status ?? "any"):\(page):\(perPage)" - no tenant component. ResponseCache.shared is one process-wide actor (ResponseCache.swift:9) with a 45s TTL. The cache is read at :45; the tenant predicate first appears at :49 and :63, on the miss path only.
findings.impact: For 45 seconds after any staff member loads the dashboard, every other staff member of every other council requesting the same status/page/perPage combination receives that council's permit list: reference, applicant name, applicant email, site address, status. The default page=1&perPage=25 collides across every tenant on the first request, so this is the steady-state behaviour of the endpoint rather than an attack that has to be mounted. `sort` is also absent from the key, so a response ordered one way is served for a request that asked for another.
findings.recommendation: Prefix the key with user.tenantID and include sort; use a delimiter the segments cannot contain, or hash the tuple. Narrow invalidate(prefix:) to the same prefix so one council's write stops flushing every council's cache.

triage.reason: The only tenant control on this path is the SQL filter at :49/:63, and the cache hit at :45-47 returns before it. BearerAuthMiddleware only calls request.auth.login.
The payload carries applicantName, applicantEmail and siteAddress - a named individual and their address.
The construct is the singleton at ResponseCache.swift:8-9 with exactly one read/write pair; nothing narrows it to one tenant.
Second principal is a staff user of a different tenant_id; multi-tenancy is established by the unique(on: tenant_id, reference) constraint and the tenant_id column on staff_users.

scope.established_by: Traced every call site of ResponseCache in the tree: value/store in list, invalidate in create, update and AdminController.approve. Only the value/store pair carries a payload.
scope.narrowed_by: listProjection (Permit.swift:71-84) blanks internalReviewNotes and reviewerEmail, so those two fields do not cross; applicant identity and site address do. The 45s TTL bounds each individual leak window but not how often it recurs.

searched.for: a per-tenant partition, per-request lifetime, or key namespace applied inside the cache
searched.found: a single entries dictionary on a static let shared actor - one namespace for the whole process

searched.for: whether the cached shape is already redacted enough to make the leak harmless
searched.found: listProjection blanks only the reviewer fields; applicant identity and address remain

searched.for: evidence that a deployment is single-tenant, which would kill the finding
searched.found: the opposite - tenant_id is a required column with a composite unique constraint, and the admin export accepts a tenant parameter

findings.title: replaceContent omits the tenant ownership check its three sibling handlers perform
findings.class: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key / OWASP API1:2023
findings.evidence: metadata (:79-85), download (:90-96) and remove (:128-134) each bind the StaffUser and then guard `permit.tenantID == user.tenantID`. replaceContent binds it to `_` at :109 and never compares. load() at :66-74 is Attachment.find(id) with no filter, and Attachment carries no tenant_id column of its own, so tenancy is reachable only through the parent permit - the lookup this handler skips.
findings.impact: Any holder of any valid staff token, in any tenant, can overwrite the bytes and declared content type of any attachment in the system with a single PUT /api/v1/attachments/<uuid>/content. On statutory permit records that is evidence tampering: the scanned plans a caseworker approves are replaced while the permit history still points at one document. The attachment UUID is the only thing needed and it is a discovery barrier, not a control - it appears in URLs, emails and browser history, and a staff member who legitimately handled a permit keeps every UUID they saw.
findings.recommendation: Add the same two-line guard the siblings use - load the parent permit and compare tenantID - before the decode. Structurally, put tenant_id on the attachments table so the scope can be enforced in one place instead of re-derived in four handlers, three of which remember.

triage.reason: BearerAuthMiddleware establishes identity only (request.auth.login at :59). No layer between the route and the sink applies a tenant scope; load() is an unfiltered find by primary key.
The three siblings enforce the check in application code, so the project's own implementation shows the control is expected here and not delegated to a platform.
The handlers do reach the same effect on the same resource family; replaceContent is the most powerful of the four and the only ungated one.
Registered unconditionally at AttachmentController.swift:61 inside the api/v1 group.

scope.established_by: Listed every handler in the collection from boot() at :56-64, then listed every place the StaffUser bound from req.auth is actually read. Three of four compare tenantID; the fourth binds to _.
scope.narrowed_by: The content-type allowlist (:113) and the 8MB size cap (:116) still apply, so the overwrite is bounded to one of four declared types - they bound the payload, not the authorization. The attachment UUID must be known.

searched.for: a tenant filter applied centrally that would make the per-handler guards redundant
searched.found: Attachment.find(id, on: req.db) - an unfiltered primary-key lookup; the guards are per-handler by construction

searched.for: a tenant_id column on attachments that would let a scope be enforced without the parent lookup
searched.found: none - permit_id only, and no foreign key constraint on it either

searched.for: a middleware that injects a tenant scope into every Fluent query and fails closed

findings.title: The applicant-register CSV export takes the tenant to dump from a query parameter
findings.class: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key / CWE-359
findings.evidence: let tenant = try req.query.get(UUID.self, at: "tenant") at :49, feeding .filter(\.$tenantID == tenant) at :51. Nothing compares that value to a session. The response is the full table, unpaged, as CSV: reference,status,applicant,site,reviewer.
findings.impact: One request returns every permit record held for a named council - applicant name and site address for the entire population, plus the reviewer assigned to each. Because the tenant comes from the parameter rather than the caller, the boundary is crossed regardless of who reaches the endpoint. Nothing is written down: the tree has exactly one logging call (configure.swift:89, a startup error), so after an incident nobody can answer whose records were read and the whole population has to be treated as affected.
findings.recommendation: Take the tenant from the authenticated session, never from the request; cap or stream the result; write an entry naming actor, tenant, row count and time for every export, to a destination the exporter cannot edit.

triage.reason: The value is read directly from the query string at :49.
Even granting the 'council LAN' comment in full, a network bound does not bound the tenant dimension: any principal that reaches the route exports any council.
Looked for a narrowing in the same block; the .filter at :51 is the opposite - it makes the parameter authoritative.
Applicant names and site addresses are direct identifiers and the location of a named person.

findings.title: Admin handlers apply no tenant or role authorization, and the role predicate is defined and never called
findings.class: CWE-862 Missing Authorization / OWASP API5:2023
findings.evidence: approve uses `Permit.find(permitID, on: req.db)` with no tenant filter, while every other read of a permit in the codebase carries .filter(\.$tenantID == user.tenantID) (PermitController.swift:80, :114, :137). StaffUser.isApprover (BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:12) has exactly one occurrence in the tree - the definition. `roles` is loaded from the database into StaffUser at :49/:60 and consulted by nothing.
findings.impact: This is the defect that survives the fix for the unauthenticated /internal group. Mounting it behind BearerAuthMiddleware still leaves every handler open to any authenticated staff account of any council: approve or refuse a permit in a different council, register attachments against a different council's permits. The dead isApprover shows a role gate was designed and never wired, so even within one council a junior clerk carries the same authority as a supervisor. Separately, asDTO returns internalReviewNotes and reviewerEmail - free-text council commentary about a named applicant - to every staff session in the tenant regardless of role.
findings.recommendation: In approve, scope the lookup with the caller's tenantID and gate on user.isApprover - the predicate already exists. Gate internalReviewNotes/reviewerEmail on isApprover at the DTO boundary, or delete the predicate so nobody reads it as a live control.

triage.reason: No layer applies a role or tenant scope. The only middleware on the path once /internal is fixed would be BearerAuthMiddleware, which logs the user in and makes no authorization decision.
The gap covers all three state-touching handlers (:29, :48, :82); it is not one route reading wider than it applies.
isApprover is compiled into the shipped binary and the handlers are registered unconditionally; the absence of a caller is not a build-time exclusion.
approve writes a legally operative status onto a permit record, and the notes field is free text about a named applicant.

scope.narrowed_by: activeSessions (:98) reads a global count and has no tenant dimension to scope, so only the role half applies to it. listProjection blanks the two commentary fields, so the browsable listing is unaffected.

findings.title: Bulk attachment import accepts a client-chosen storageKey and contentType, breaking the model's documented invariant
findings.class: CWE-639 / OWASP API1:2023 (identifiers named in the request body)
findings.evidence: Lines 85-92 assign attachment.contentType = row.contentType and attachment.storageKey = row.storageKey directly from the decoded body, consulting neither PermitController.allowedUploadTypes nor BlobStore.resolve. Permit.swift:29-30 documents the opposite invariant: 'Server-assigned. Uploads never influence where bytes land on disk.' The normal upload path does enforce both (PermitController.swift:144-154, server-generated UUID key).
findings.impact: Three effects from one untrusted field. (1) Cross-tenant blob read: register a row whose permitID is your own permit and whose storageKey is another council's; download's tenant check inspects the parent permit - yours - and passes, then serves their document. This survives fixing the auth and tenant defects, because scoping permitID does nothing to storageKey. (2) Arbitrary content type served inline from the API origin: this is the one write path that skips allowedUploadTypes, and download echoes the stored contentType with Content-Disposition: inline and no X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. (3) Deleted documents return: remove deletes the index row and never the blob, so a 'deleted' key can be re-registered and downloaded again.
findings.recommendation: Generate the storage key server-side on import as the upload path does, or at minimum run it through BlobStore.resolve and verify the caller owns both the permit and the key. Apply allowedUploadTypes on this path too. Add nosniff to the download response, delete the blob in remove, and stop returning storageKey in the JSON.

triage.reason: storageKey and contentType are decoded straight from the request body into ImportedAttachment (:11-17, :83) and assigned without transformation.
Naming another row's storage key is not inert - it is what the download handler dereferences at AttachmentController.swift:98.
BlobStore.resolve is the shape control and the import path never calls it; the download path calls it on a key this handler chose, which validates shape and not ownership.

scope.established_by: Followed each field of ImportedAttachment from the decode at :83 to its persisted column, then forward from the column to every reader of that column in the tree.
scope.narrowed_by: BlobStore.resolve still runs on the read (AttachmentController.swift:34), so the key cannot traverse out of the blob root - it can only name a different file inside it. That bounds this to cross-tenant blob read, not arbitrary file read.

searched.for: whether the codebase's own upload path validates what import does not
searched.found: it does - allowlist at :144, size cap at :147, server-generated UUID key at :154. The import path is the asymmetric one.

searched.for: a check that the storage key belongs to the permit whose tenant was just verified
searched.found: none - the key is dereferenced as stored, so the permit->tenant check and the key are decoupled

searched.for: blob deletion that would prevent re-registration of a deleted key
searched.found: only attachment.delete(on: req.db); the bytes stay on disk

findings.title: The rate-limit bucket is keyed on the caller's own unverified bearer token
findings.class: CWE-837 Improper Enforcement of a Single, Unique Action / CWE-770 / OWASP API4:2023
findings.evidence: identity() returns "tok:" + String(bearer.token.prefix(16)) from request.headers.bearerAuthorization. routes.swift:37-38 applies the limiter as the OUTER middleware, so it runs before BearerAuthMiddleware validates anything.
findings.impact: The counter key is a value the caller chooses. Sending a different random 16-character bearer token on each request produces a fresh Redis key with a count of 1 every time, so the 120/minute limit never fires for anyone who does not want it to. Token brute-force against BearerAuthMiddleware is therefore entirely unthrottled, and every rejected attempt still costs a Postgres round trip on an indexed join before the 401 - so the limiter also fails as a resource-exhaustion control on exactly the surface it was placed to protect. The IP fallback at :40 is unreachable for anyone sending any Authorization header.
findings.recommendation: Bucket after authentication, on the resolved StaffUser.id. A pre-auth bucket must key on something the caller does not control (the peer address), never on the credential being tested.

triage.reason: One limiter in the tree, registered once at routes.swift:37. No second counter and no per-account lockout: StaffDirectory.verify keeps no attempt state.
The bucket string is request.headers.bearerAuthorization, read before any validation; its value is entirely attacker-chosen.
identity() is the sole key source for the middleware and the middleware covers the whole api/v1 subtree.

scope.established_by: Read the middleware's only key-producing function and joined it against the registration order in routes.swift, which determines whether the token has been validated when the key is built.
scope.narrowed_by: Requests with no Authorization header fall to the peer-address bucket at :40, which is sound - the defect is confined to callers who send the header.

searched.for: an edge-proxy control that would compensate
searched.found: the comment claims the proxy normalises client-supplied forwarding headers. That is about the IP path and says nothing about a proxy-side rate limit; no such artifact is in scope.

searched.for: an account lockout or attempt counter that would blunt brute force independently of the limiter
searched.found: neither; verify() returns nil three times and records nothing

findings.title: The credential endpoint sits outside the rate-limited group
findings.class: CWE-307 Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
findings.evidence: app.post("auth","token") is registered on the bare Application at :22; the rate-limited group is not constructed until :35. No global middleware in configure.swift:52-65 limits anything.
findings.impact: Unlimited unauthenticated password attempts against a council staff directory, with no lockout anywhere in the system (StaffDirectory.verify records nothing). Bcrypt slows a single guess but does not stop password spraying, which is the realistic attack: a handful of common passwords across every staff email address. The same property is an amplifier in the other direction - each attempt costs a full bcrypt verification of server CPU, so an unauthenticated caller can saturate the process with concurrent requests to this one route.
findings.recommendation: Apply the limiter to this route with a small limit keyed on peer address and on the submitted username, and add per-account lockout with a counter that survives process restart.

triage.reason: The limiter is registered exactly once, at routes.swift:37 on the api/v1 group; /auth/token is registered on the bare Application at :22.
The endpoint is intentionally public, but 'public' bounds who may call it, not how often. Nothing bounds the rate.
This is an absence at one route, not a wide construct whose reach might be narrower than it reads.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all mount points and joined them against the single limiter registration: /healthz, /auth/token and the whole /internal subtree are outside it; only api/v1 is inside.
scope.narrowed_by: /healthz is also unmetered but returns a constant; /internal is carried by its own finding.

searched.found: CORS, ErrorMiddleware and FileMiddleware only

findings.title: CORS falls back to a wildcard origin, governed by a second and independent notion of production
findings.class: CWE-942 Permissive Cross-domain Policy / CWE-1188 Insecure Default Initialization
findings.evidence: let portalEnv = Environment.get("PORTAL_ENV") ?? "staging" at :46, then a ternary at :48-50 selecting .all whenever portalEnv != "production". The middleware is registered globally at :52 with allowedMethods including POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, allowedHeaders including contentType, and allowCredentials: true. Eleven lines later, :70 uses Vapor's own app.environment for a different decision.
findings.impact: The credentialed-read story is NOT real and I am not reporting it: .all emits a literal *, and browsers refuse * together with credentials. What is real is the preflight. The wildcard plus POST/PUT/DELETE plus content-type makes the preflight succeed for any origin, which is what lets an arbitrary website deliver a cross-origin JSON body to the unauthenticated /internal write endpoints from a browser inside the council network - without it, a no-preflight simple request cannot carry a content type Vapor will decode as JSON. The ?? "staging" default means a deployment that sets --env production and forgets PORTAL_ENV gets the permissive branch with no signal.
findings.recommendation: Default to the restrictive branch and make the permissive one require explicit opt-in; better, drive it from app.environment so there is one notion of production. Drop allowCredentials unless a cookie path exists - this API authorizes on the Authorization header only.

triage.reason: Whether the shipped deployment sets PORTAL_ENV=production is not decidable from the files in scope - no Dockerfile, manifest, chart or CI configuration was provided. This caps the finding at probable; the source-level defect (the insecure branch is the default) is confirmed.
This is the shape FP-11 exists for and it does not save the finding: app.middleware.use at :52 applies the middleware to every response from every route, not to one handler.
No layer re-checks the origin; CORSMiddleware is the outermost registered middleware, so even ErrorMiddleware responses carry its headers.
The responses the wildcard exposes include the /internal export and the /internal write endpoints.

scope.narrowed_by: portalEnv == "production" narrows it to deployments that do not set that variable - which, given the ?? "staging" default, is every deployment that does not set it deliberately.

searched.for: whether PORTAL_ENV and Vapor's own environment are kept in sync anywhere
searched.found: they are not - two independent switches, and the migration decision uses app.environment while the CORS decision uses PORTAL_ENV

findings.title: Deleting an attachment removes the index row and leaves the document on disk
findings.class: CWE-212 Improper Removal of Sensitive Information Before Storage or Transfer / CWE-459
findings.evidence: try await attachment.delete(on: req.db) is the whole of the deletion. BlobStore (:13-48) declares put, get and putRestored and no delete; grep for BlobStore across the component returns five call sites, none a removal.
findings.impact: Every permit document ever uploaded stays under BLOB_ROOT indefinitely, including those an applicant or caseworker believes are gone - the data at rest outlives the record that pointed at it, with no expiry and no inventory. Permit attachments are applicant-submitted documents; the allowed types are pdf/png/jpeg/csv, i.e. scans.

findings.title: The listing's status filter is built and never reaches the query

findings.evidence: Lines 49-52 build `var query = Permit.query(...).filter(tenantID)` and conditionally add .filter(status). Lines 61-66 then execute a different raw SQL statement whose WHERE clause carries tenant_id only. The `query` binding is assigned at :49, reassigned at :51 and never read again.

findings.title: ExportItems runs with no authentication and takes its tenant from a client-supplied header
findings.class: CWE-306 Missing Authentication for Critical Function / CWE-807 / OWASP API1:2023+API5:2023
findings.evidence: main.go:50-59 passes grpc.UnaryInterceptor(auth.Unary) and no stream interceptor; a tree-wide grep for StreamInterceptor/ChainStream returns nothing. ExportItems is declared `returns (stream Item)` in catalog.proto:81, so AuthInterceptor.Unary never runs for it. server.go:204 is `caller, _ := CallerFrom(ctx)` - the one call site of six that discards ok - so caller.TenantID is always empty and the fallback at :210, metadataValue(ctx, "x-catalog-tenant"), is the sole tenant source.
findings.impact: credentials.NewServerTLSFromFile (main.go:40) is server-side TLS with ClientAuth at its NoClientCert default, and the listener binds :8443 on all interfaces. Anyone who can open a TCP connection to the gRPC port, holding no token at all, streams the complete catalogue of any tenant they name - the RPC the proto itself calls 'download everything'. No role check either, so RequireRole is absent from the one RPC that returns the most data. Composed with the ExportQuery injection below, this is a pre-authentication arbitrary read of the database.
findings.recommendation: Register grpc.StreamInterceptor with a Stream method performing the same resolve as Unary, and wrap the stream so the handler sees the authenticated context. Treat ok == false from CallerFrom as Unauthenticated and delete the x-catalog-tenant fallback entirely; give the nightly scheduler its own per-tenant service credential.

findings.title: SQL injection in ExportQuery: filter, order and tenant are interpolated, not bound
findings.class: CWE-89 SQL Injection / OWASP A05:2025 / WSTG-INPV-05
findings.evidence: search.go:99-113 sets where = filter with no parse and no allowlist, then fmt.Sprintf(`... WHERE tenant_id = '%s' AND (%s) ORDER BY %s`, tenantID, where, order). postgres.go:225-226 executes it as p.pool.Query(ctx, query) with zero variadic args, so nothing can bind. The sibling path proves the tree knows better: Search sends the same class of input through ParseFilter/ParseOrderBy and reaches postgres.go:203 with args...
findings.impact: The three parameters arrive from ExportRequest.filter, ExportRequest.order_by and the tenant resolved at server.go:206-211. The tenant predicate is defeated by a filter of `TRUE) OR (TRUE`, and the nine-column SELECT is a ready-made UNION target for any table the pool's role can read - including api_sessions, i.e. subject, tenant and role for every live session. ORDER BY %s accepts a subquery for boolean/timing extraction, and pg_sleep in that position is a cheap denial of service. pgx v5's default extended-protocol exec mode means stacked statements do not execute, so impact is arbitrary read plus DoS rather than arbitrary write. Chained with the missing stream interceptor this is pre-authentication.
findings.recommendation: Route the export through the same ParseFilter/ParseOrderBy that Search already uses, and change StreamQuery to take (query string, args []any) so the tenant and every literal bind. The signature accepting a pre-built statement is itself the hazard.

triage.reason: ParseFilter and ParseOrderBy are the allowlists and ExportQuery calls neither; server.go:216 passes req.GetFilter()/req.GetOrderBy() raw. postgres.go:226 executes with no argument slice, so no binding can occur downstream.

filter and order_by are proto string fields on ExportRequest read at server.go:216; tenantID is either the session tenant or the x-catalog-tenant header. At least two of the three are attacker-controlled on every call.

The sink is pgxpool.Query - a statement executor, not a parser. The extended protocol blocks stacked statements, which bounds the finding to read and DoS; it does not make the sink safe, because the injected text still changes the WHERE and ORDER BY of the executed statement.

Checked whether the construct applies to less than it looks like: the tenant_id predicate is the narrowing condition, and it is inside the injectable string rather than outside it, so the injection dissolves the very thing that would have narrowed it.

findings.title: The caller chooses its own role: x-catalog-role metadata overwrites the session role
findings.class: CWE-807 Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision / CWE-269 / OWASP API5:2023
findings.evidence: Lines 62-69: the authenticated Caller is built from session.Subject/TenantID/Role, then `if role := metadataValue(ctx, "x-catalog-role"); role != "" { caller.Role = role }`. RequireRole at :94-100 then compares caller.Role against a literal list - the comparison is sound; its input is not.
findings.impact: The tenant is taken from the credential and the role is taken from the wire, in adjacent lines. Any holder of any valid session - the lowest-privileged read-only account - attaches x-catalog-role: admin to a unary call and satisfies every authorization gate in the service: DeleteItem (admin-only), CreateItem/UpdateItem (editor-or-admin), and the publish gates reserving VISIBILITY_PUBLIC for admins. That is complete vertical escalation to destructive operations with a single header. The comment explains the intent - the console disambiguating among several roles a session holds - but the implementation places no relationship between the asserted role and the session's actual roles, so it grants rather than narrows.
findings.recommendation: Derive Role from the session only. If the console needs to act under one of several held roles, store the role set in api_sessions, treat x-catalog-role as a request to NARROW to a member of that set, and reject with PermissionDenied when the asserted role is not in it - never widen.

triage.reason: RequireRole is the compensating control and it is invoked at server.go:76,114,153. It compares caller.Role, which line 67 has already replaced with the client's string. A control downstream of the corruption is not a control over it.
metadataValue reads md.Get("x-catalog-role") from the incoming gRPC metadata - written by the peer. Traced backwards it terminates at the client.

Asked specifically whether the override is narrower than it reads. There is no check on session.Role, no membership test, no peer-identity condition, no environment gate. The only guard is role != "".
The header's stated purpose is role selection among roles the caller already holds, which requires a bound to the session that the code does not implement.

scope.established_by: Traced Caller.Role from its authenticated source (interceptor.go:62) to every consumer (RequireRole at server.go:76,114,153; the publish gates at :87,:122), then back to the last write before those reads, which is line 67.
scope.narrowed_by: Applies to every unary RPC, since resolve() runs for all of them. Through the HTTP gateway the escalation is reachable but inert, because only GetItem and Search are mounted and neither consults Role; the exploitable surface is the direct gRPC listener.

findings.title: The HTTP gateway's stripped-header table omits the one privilege-bearing header it forwards
findings.class: CWE-348 Use of Less Trusted Source / CWE-807
findings.evidence: forwardedPrefixes at :23 includes "x-catalog-", so outgoingContext copies every x-catalog-* request header onto the gRPC call. strippedHeaders at :27-30 removes x-catalog-tenant and x-catalog-subject and nothing else. x-catalog-role - the header the interceptor uses to set the caller's role - is not in the table.
findings.impact: The two most obvious siblings are blocked and the third is not, which is the signature of an incomplete denylist rather than a considered decision. Any HTTP caller of the JSON gateway can set x-catalog-role and have it forwarded into the gRPC metadata the interceptor reads. It is reported separately from the interceptor defect because it is an independent lapse at a different layer with its own fix, and because the table is the artefact a maintainer will consult when adding the next x-catalog-* header. Its practical reach today is bounded: only GetItem and Search are mounted in the gateway mux, and neither consults Role - so fixing the interceptor neutralises this, while fixing this alone leaves the interceptor exploitable over direct gRPC.
findings.recommendation: Invert the table to an allowlist of headers the gateway may forward, so the next x-catalog-* header is denied by default rather than forwarded by default. Add x-catalog-role explicitly in the meantime.

triage.reason: The interceptor is the layer that consumes the header and it applies no provenance check; there is no other filter between the HTTP request and the gRPC metadata.
The value is r.Header on an inbound HTTP request - client-written.

The reach is genuinely narrower than the construct suggests: only two RPCs are mounted in the gateway mux and neither reads Caller.Role, so through this path the forwarded header is inert today. That narrowing is why this is medium and not high, and it does not delete the finding, because the table is what the next mounted RPC will inherit.

scope.narrowed_by: Only GetItem and Search are mounted in the gateway; neither consults Caller.Role, so the escalation through this path is latent rather than live.

findings.title: The item cache is keyed by item id alone, so a cache hit skips the tenant predicate
findings.class: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key / CWE-524 / OWASP API1:2023
findings.evidence: server.go:52-56 returns `s.Cache.Get(req.GetId())` before the tenant-scoped read at :58 (`s.Store.GetItem(ctx, caller.TenantID, req.GetId())`). The Put at :67 also keys on the bare id. cache.go is a flat map with no tenant component: cacheEntry holds only value and storedAt.
findings.impact: ItemCache is a single process-wide map (main.go:63) and all four call sites key on the bare item id. The tenant scope lives exclusively in the SQL at postgres.go:90, and the early return is upstream of it. Once tenant A reads an item, any authenticated caller in any other tenant issuing GetItem for that id within the 90-second TTL receives the row in full - sku, title, description, price - with the tenant control silently bypassed. findings.title: Idempotency keys share one global namespace, and the collision error returns another tenant's item id
findings.class: CWE-209 Information Exposure Through an Error Message / CWE-639 / OWASP API3:2023
findings.evidence: Schema at :31-35 declares create_receipts with idempotency_key text PRIMARY KEY and no tenant column, while items carries a tenant-scoped unique index at :29. The lookup at :104-107 has no tenant predicate, and the failure returns fmt.Errorf("idempotency key already used for item %s", existing) - handed to the caller verbatim by server.go:104 as status.Errorf(codes.AlreadyExists, "%v", err).
findings.impact: Two problems on one line of SQL. The receipts table is keyed by the client-chosen string alone, so a key another tenant has used makes a legitimate create fail - a cross-tenant denial needing only a colliding string, and idempotency keys are frequently derived from something guessable such as an order reference. Second, the failure discloses item_id: a UUID belonging to whichever tenant used the key first. That id is precisely the missing precondition for the cache defect above, so the two compose into a cross-tenant read that needs no other information. The same passthrough shape sits at server.go:141, where any non-ErrNotFound error from UpdateItem - including raw pgx text carrying constraint and column names - is returned as InvalidArgument.
findings.recommendation: Make the receipt key composite - PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, idempotency_key) - and add the tenant predicate to the lookup. On collision, replay the original response as the idempotency contract intends, or return a bare AlreadyExists with no identifier. Replace both "%v" passthroughs with a fixed message plus a correlation id.

triage.reason: Looked for an error-mapping layer between the store and the wire. server.go:104 formats the store error directly into the status message; the interceptor passes handler results through untouched.
The disclosed value is a live items.id of another tenant. Its security value is established inside this tree: it is the exact input the cache defect needs, and GetItem accepts it.
idempotency_key is CreateItemRequest.idempotency_key, passed at server.go:102 with no normalisation between the wire and the primary-key lookup.
Considered downgrading to informational on the grounds that it is only an error string. It is not defence in depth: the message is the sole disclosure channel and it emits a usable identifier.

findings.evidence: All three legs are on one agent. Untrusted ingestion: searchChunks at :28 returns text crawled from four third-party hosts (crawler.ts:9-14). Private data: the same call, plus the search_corpus tool. Outbound channel: share_document (tools.ts:94) POSTs with a model-chosen `to` and `note`, and open_ticket (tools.ts:112) POSTs 4000 characters of model-chosen detail. The dispatcher at loop.ts:66-87 runs whatever the model named and passes model-authored arguments straight through; grep for interrupt|require_approval|confirm|approval across src/ returns nothing.

Nothing in this tree constrains the recipient or the body, and the user never sees the tool arguments - only toolsUsed, a list of names. The recipient parameter's whole specification is `{ type: 'string', description: 'Email address to send it to' }`, so there is no allowlist, no domain check and no confirmation.

Drop share_document's free-text note and take the recipient from a server-side allowlist keyed to the workspace, never from model output. Put every outbound tool behind a confirmation that renders the literal arguments. A recipient allowlist inside the notify service would close one sub-path of one tool; it would not rule out the finding as scoped, since open_ticket's free-text detail and the private-data leg survive it.

findings.title: Retrieved third-party content is interpolated into the system message with no delimitation or provenance
findings.evidence: prompt.ts:29-38 builds one role:'system' message as HOUSE_RULES + workspace/plan + '## Context' + renderContext(chunks). renderContext at :12-16 emits `### Source ${index+1} — ${chunk.label} (${chunk.url})\n${chunk.text}` with no escaping of any of the three interpolated values. The chunk text is whatever stripMarkup (crawler.ts:27-36) left of a third-party HTML page: it removes tags but keeps the text of CSS-hidden elements, decodes only four named entities, and no Unicode normalisation runs anywhere on the path.
findings.impact: Instructions written into a partner documentation page enter the model's context in the system role - the highest-authority plane - indistinguishable from the house rules three lines above them. Because chunk.text is interpolated unescaped, a chunk can also forge its own `### Source` delimiter and attribute injected text to a fabricated source. The label (120 chars, admin-supplied) and the URL path are equally unescaped, giving anyone who can call corpus.crawl a newline-injection route into the prompt structure. This is the mechanism that makes the trifecta exploitable. Detection is also weak: chunks carry url/label but no trust level and retrieval filters on neither.
findings.recommendation: Spotlighting. Move retrieved passages out of the system message into a separate, explicitly labelled data turn; delimit each chunk with a random per-request sentinel and strip that sentinel from the chunk text; escape or reject '#', newlines and the sentinel in label and url before interpolation; normalise Unicode and strip invisible ranges at ingest. Store a trust level per document and make retrieval filter on it.

triage.reason: No sanitiser, delimiter or spotlighting step exists between weaviate.ts:69-75 and prompt.ts:14. redactChunk runs at ingest and targets PII, not instructions.

The exculpation requires an immutable internal corpus with no external write path. crawler.ts:9-14 makes the corpus explicitly external - four third-party HTTPS hosts whose content their owners control.
The construct is exactly what it looks like: a template literal placing network-sourced text inside a message whose role field is the string 'system'.

scope.narrowed_by: Nothing - there is no branch, flag or plan on which the context is delimited.

findings.title: Tool output is re-injected as a system message, with the tool name interpolated unescaped

findings.title: Crawler host allowlist is enforced on the first hop only; redirects are followed unvalidated
findings.class: CWE-918 Server-Side Request Forgery / LLM05:2026
findings.evidence: Line 44 checks parsed.protocol and ALLOWED_HOSTS.has(parsed.hostname) against the URL as submitted, built once at :43. The request at :48-52 passes maxRedirections: 2, and undici follows those hops with no host or scheme constraint of its own; the application re-validates nothing per hop. crawler.ts:69 then stores parsed.toString() - the original approved URL - as the chunk provenance.
findings.impact: An admin-triggered crawl of an approved URL that answers 302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/... or http://weaviate.internal:8080/v1/objects fetches that internal resource and writes its body into the workspace corpus, where any member reads it back through chat.search and where the agent reads it as system-plane context. The allowlist is the only control between a privileged-but-not-omnipotent admin and the internal network, and it does not cover the hop that matters. Two aggravators: the stored provenance names the approved host, so internal content is labelled as coming from a partner portal; and :58-61 buffers the entire response with body.text() before testing raw.length > MAX_BYTES, so a redirect to an unbounded stream is an in-process memory exhaustion with no cap at all.
findings.recommendation: Set maxRedirections: 0 and follow hops manually, re-running the protocol and ALLOWED_HOSTS check on every Location; resolve the hostname and reject private, loopback, link-local and unique-local addresses before connecting, re-checking after resolution to close the rebinding window; record the final URL as provenance; stream the body and abort at MAX_BYTES instead of buffering first; set an explicit request timeout.

triage.reason: The exculpation would be that the fetched URL is constrained by an allowlist before reaching the sink. It is - for hop 1 only. The value that reaches the actual request on hop 2 is the Location header, controlled by whoever operates the approved host.

Looked for a narrowing condition that would make the allowlist cover the whole chain: the check operates on `parsed`, a URL object built once at :43 and never rebuilt, and undici's redirect handling is internal to the request call.
An egress proxy or network policy in front of this process would blunt it, and no such artifact is in scope. This caps the finding at probable.

findings.title: Chunk redaction is enforced at a caller rather than at the writer, and misses the printed IBAN form
findings.class: CWE-359 Exposure of Private Information / CWE-212
findings.evidence: The IBAN rule is /\b[A-Z]{2}\d{2}[A-Z0-9]{11,30}\b/g - no i flag and no tolerance for separators, so the human-readable grouped-by-four form and any lowercase one do not match; the sibling NI_NUMBER rule carries gi, which makes the omission legible as an oversight. redactChunk has exactly one call site, crawler.ts:64, and the writer it protects, indexChunks (weaviate.ts:31), does no redaction of its own. The docstring at :6-9 asserts 'Everything indexed has been through here, so retrieval never has to worry about it again.'

findings.class: CWE-295 Improper Certificate Validation / CWE-1188 / CWE-319

findings.title: The /auth route bypasses forwardAuth, so client-supplied identity headers reach the upstream unstripped
findings.class: CWE-290 Authentication Bypass by Spoofing / CWE-807 / CWE-863
findings.evidence: licensing-api at :6-15 carries middlewares [fleet-auth, api-ratelimit, compress]; licensing-auth at :17-24 carries only [compress]. Both resolve to the same service, licensing-api (:9, :19, :66-70). A request to /auth/... carrying X-Fleet-Role: admin and an arbitrary X-Fleet-Tenant is therefore a privilege-escalation and cross-tenant-access primitive on an internet-facing government licensing API, reachable unauthenticated. Marked probable because the upstream's handling of these headers on /auth paths is not in this component.

Keep fleet-auth off /auth as intended; the stripper is what makes that safe.

It does not: Traefik's Del/Set of authResponseHeaders happens inside the forwardAuth middleware instance, so it covers exactly the two routers that list fleet-auth.

findings.title: The log redaction transform cannot fire on the input that carries raw task output
findings.class: CWE-532 Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File / A09:2025
findings.evidence: redact takes inputs ["parse_access", "nomad_alloc_logs"] at :24, but its two conditions test .request.headers.authorization (:26) and .response.headers."set-cookie" (:29) - fields that unparsed file-source events do not have. Only parse_access (:12-18) produces a structured event; nomad_alloc_logs (:3-6) is a raw file source whose payload is a string in .message. Separately, the gateway_access source globs a traefik/local/access.log that nothing writes, because edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:56 sets --accesslog=true with no --accesslog.filepath, so Traefik logs to stdout; and :17 reads get_env_var!("NOMAD_CLIENT_ID"), a variable the job never defines.
findings.impact: The stated guarantee at :20-21 is that credentials never reach the shared log bucket. For every allocation's stdout and stderr on every node - the larger input by far - the redaction is a guaranteed no-op and whatever a task prints goes verbatim to s3://fleet-platform-logs. That includes the node running ledger-db, whose Postgres writes failing statements to stderr with bound parameters, which on this workload are bank account numbers; the reconcile flow's own code shows those failures are routine. read_from = "beginning" means a Vector restart re-ships from the head of each file, and no lifecycle or expiry is declared anywhere in the component.
findings.recommendation: Redact by pattern on .message for the file-sourced input rather than by structured field paths it does not have, or parse alloc logs into the same shape before redacting. Set --accesslog.filepath on Traefik or point the source at the real stdout path, replace get_env_var! with a name the job defines, and assert the guarantee with a test event on each input rather than in a comment.

triage.reason: The candidate compensating control is --accesslog.fields.headers.defaultmode=drop, and it does hold for the Authorization header in the access log specifically - which is why this is medium and not high. It does not cover application stdout, which is the larger input.

All three deployments inherit it, including reconcile-nightly on the production work pool with LEDGER_DSN injected from the production secret block, and drain-settlement-notices every 300 seconds on the same pool.
findings.impact: What production executes tonight is whatever main points at tonight. Anyone who can land a commit on main - or anyone who compromises the internal git host - executes arbitrary code against the production ledger database on the next tick, with no release, no approval and no artifact to compare afterwards. The second principal is anyone with write access to the internal repository, who is not necessarily anyone entitled to production ledger credentials; the deployment grants the latter to the former with no gate.
findings.recommendation: Pin the pull step to an immutable reference - a commit_sha, or at minimum a signed tag the deployment process moves deliberately - and pair it with branch protection and review on main so the pinned reference is also an approved one.

triage.reason: The 'same owner and access-control perimeter' exculpation does not apply cleanly: write access to the repository and entitlement to production ledger credentials are different populations here.

Branch protection on the internal git host would materially reduce this, and no repository settings, ruleset export or CI configuration exists anywhere in the corpus to establish it either way. This caps the finding at probable.
This is not an absent attestation over an otherwise-verified artifact; there is no artifact and no verification anywhere on the path.

scope.narrowed_by: Nothing - no deployment overrides the pull step.

searched.found: none; all three inherit the single file-level pull step

searched.found: no CI configuration of any kind, and no verification step - which is also why the finding is probable

findings.title: The desktop app ships an Electron major that left support, and the caret cannot leave it
findings.class: CWE-1104 Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components / CWE-1395
findings.evidence: "electron": "^29.1.5". Electron supports the latest three majors; the 29 series (Chromium 122) fell out of that window in 2024. A caret on 29.1.5 resolves to >=29.1.5 <30.0.0, so this is not a stale-lockfile problem: a clean install today still installs an unsupported Electron, and there is no lockfile to pin anything else.
findings.impact: The shipped browser engine carries every Chromium and V8 fix since Chromium 122, including renderer RCEs that appear in the KEV catalog. Reachability is established rather than assumed: windows.js:67 loads remote report URLs and windows.js:34-43 permits in-window navigation to the two portal origins, so remote web content is rendered by that engine. Rated medium rather than high for one reason: in this tree the report window already runs with nodeIntegration and no sandbox, so an attacker reaching that page does not need a renderer exploit at all. This becomes the load-bearing control the moment that window is fixed - a sandbox on an unsupported Chromium is a sandbox with published escapes - so it should be upgraded in the same change.
findings.recommendation: Move to a supported Electron major, commit a lockfile so the resolved version is auditable, and put the upgrade on a schedule tied to Electron's release cadence rather than to feature work.

triage.reason: The tempting answer is that a devDependency does not ship. That is wrong for this package: electron is the runtime electron-builder packages into the distributable, driven by the build block and main. The devDependency IS the shipped artifact.
No compensating layer in-tree. The sandbox that would be the natural one is explicitly off for the window that loads remote content.

The only out-of-repo control that could apply is a self-maintained patched fork. The manifest resolves from the public registry with a caret; there is no resolutions field, no overrides, and no .npmrc anywhere in the corpus.
Not an absent defence in depth - the engine is the primary control against hostile web content, and the app renders hostile-capable content.

scope.established_by: Reading the version range against Electron's published support window, then establishing that remote content reaches the engine via windows.js:34-43 and :67.
scope.narrowed_by: The caret ceiling at <30.0.0 removes the usual 'an install would pick up the fix' escape. Severity is held at medium because the isolation defect on the report window currently dominates it.

searched.for: evidence the app only ever renders local content, which would bound the engine exposure to bundled HTML
searched.found: the opposite: createMainWindow loads a local file but allows navigation to two remote portal origins, and createReportWindow calls loadURL on a caller-supplied URL

searched.looked_in: the whole corpus for .npmrc, overrides, resolutions or a vendored electron
searched.for: a private registry or pin that would mean this range does not resolve to public Electron 29
searched.found: nothing - no registry configuration exists in any of the six components

findings.title: The tRPC server dependency is pinned to a floating prerelease range
findings.class: CWE-1357 Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component / CWE-829
findings.evidence: "@trpc/server": "^11.0.0-rc.400". Under node-semver a caret on a prerelease means >=11.0.0-rc.400 <12.0.0 - it floats across every later release candidate and onward into the stable 11.x line. There is no package-lock.json in this component, so nothing fixes the resolution.
findings.impact: The range spans a stability boundary: an rc line makes no compatibility promise between candidates, so two installs a week apart can put materially different code on the request path. And the package is on that path - server.ts:1-2 uses initTRPC, TRPCError and createHTTPServer, and server.ts:29/43/59 is the authorization chain (authedProcedure, meteredProcedure, adminProcedure). A malicious or merely broken release in the 11.x line is adopted automatically at the next install, with no review step and no integrity record of what was installed last time.
findings.recommendation: Pin @trpc/server to an exact version and commit package-lock.json; move to the stable 11.x line deliberately rather than by drift. Install with npm ci in every environment.

triage.reason: The stated exculpation is a committed lock plus npm ci, which would make resolution deterministic. Neither exists: no lockfile in docwise-assist and no CI configuration at all.
Bounded to low: no exploitable condition is demonstrated in the versions this range resolves to today. It is a pinning defect on a security-relevant package, not a live vulnerability.
It is a dependencies entry, not devDependencies, and scripts.start runs the built server that imports it.

scope.established_by: Enumerating the dependencies block key by key and resolving each range; only this one is a prerelease.
scope.narrowed_by: The other four dependency ranges are stable-major carets and are covered by the lockfile finding, not here.

searched.looked_in: docwise-assist/ for package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock
searched.for: the committed lock that is the stated exculpation
searched.found: none - find over the entire corpus returns no lockfile of any kind in any component

searched.for: whether @trpc/server is reachable at runtime or merely a type-level import that would bound the impact
searched.found: reachable and load-bearing: createHTTPServer is the server itself and the auth context is built inside it

findings.title: No component commits a lockfile, and the one manifest with exact pins has no hashes

location.symbol: dependency pinning across all six components

findings.class: CWE-1357 / CWE-494 / CWE-345 non-deterministic resolution
findings.evidence: find over the whole corpus returns no package-lock.json, no go.sum, no Package.resolved and no lockfile of any kind. Per ecosystem: requirements.txt pins all six direct dependencies with == but carries no --hash entries, so the transitive closure resolves freely; Package.swift uses open `from:` ranges on all five dependencies; both package.json files use carets throughout; go.mod versions are exact by construction but with no go.sum the module content is not recorded.
findings.impact: What actually gets installed is decided at install time and is not recorded anywhere, so a compromised release in any direct or transitive dependency is adopted silently and no one can later say what a given build contained. This is the substrate under the Electron and tRPC findings rather than an independent attack path, which is why it is low: acting on it is a week of hygiene work, not an incident. Go is materially less exposed - versions are exact and the public checksum database still applies - so the severity is set by the weakest case rather than the worst-sounding one.
findings.recommendation: Commit a lockfile per ecosystem and install from it: npm ci, pip install --require-hashes against a pip-compile --generate-hashes output, a committed Package.resolved, and go.sum tracked.

triage.reason: The construct may not be what it looks like. No .git directory exists in this corpus and the absence is perfectly uniform across six components in five ecosystems, which is at least as consistent with lockfiles being excluded from the extract as with a project that commits none. I cannot distinguish the two, so this ships as probable and as one finding rather than five.
The exculpation is an internal proxy or registry freezing versions. No .npmrc, pip.conf, GOPROXY setting or registry configuration exists anywhere in the corpus.
This is about what ships, not about a path that does not.

scope.established_by: find over the entire corpus for every lockfile name in the five ecosystems present, returning none; then reading each manifest's pinning style key by key.
scope.narrowed_by: go.mod is materially less exposed than the rest, which is why the severity is set by the weakest case rather than the worst-sounding one.

searched.looked_in: the whole corpus: find for *lock*, go.sum, Package.resolved, .npmrc, pip.conf, Dockerfile, any CI yml
searched.for: either a committed lock, or the install command that would show whether a lock is bypassed
searched.found: none of them. The install command cannot be located, which is the other half of why this is probable.

searched.looked_in: docwise-assist/package.json and sitewatch-desktop/package.json, private and main keys
searched.for: the library exculpation - a publishable library legitimately does not commit a lock
searched.found: both are private: true applications, so the exculpation does not apply to either

findings.title: Every container image is referenced by mutable tag rather than by digest
findings.class: CWE-829 Inclusion of Functionality from an Untrusted Control Sphere (mutable reference)
findings.evidence: traefik:v3.0 (edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:51), postgres:16.2-alpine (ledger-db.nomad.hcl:46), timberio/vector:0.36.1-alpine (telemetry-agent.nomad.hcl:42), and registry.internal.example/ledger/flows:2.19-slim twice in prefect.yaml (:18, :23). No @sha256: anywhere in the tree - while both Nomad artifact stanzas DO pin their config files by sha256, so the discipline is understood and stops at the images.
findings.impact: traefik:v3.0 is the sharpest: a minor-series tag that upstream repoints on every 3.0.x release, on the container that terminates TLS for everything arriving from the internet. The other three are patch-level tags, still mutable but narrow. Separately from the same enumeration: prefect.yaml:18 and :23 are the SAME image reference for the production and staging pools, so there is no artifact boundary between the two environments - a push that lands for staging lands in production. Kept at low because all five point at either upstream official images or the organisation's own registry, and because digest-pinning without an update process trades this risk for an unpatched-image one.
findings.recommendation: Pin by digest and adopt an updater that moves the digests deliberately; give production and staging distinct image references so the two environments cannot share an artifact by accident.

triage.reason: Partially, and this is what caps the severity: the internal registry is inside the same access-control perimeter, which makes those two references pending hardening rather than third-party risk. It does not extend to traefik/postgres/timberio, which are public upstream tags - so the finding survives at reduced severity.
Bounded to low. This is a defence in depth that is absent but not load-bearing: no attack path in this tree depends on it, and the compensating risk of freezing digests is real.
No admission controller, image policy or signature verification exists anywhere in the corpus to constrain what a repointed tag would deploy.

scope.established_by: grep for every image reference across both infrastructure components; all five enumerated.
scope.narrowed_by: The two prefect.yaml references are the organisation's own registry; the three Nomad ones are public upstream.

searched.looked_in: edge-fleet-nomad/ for a cosign verify, Nomad image policy, or admission control
searched.for: a verification step that would make tag mutability moot
searched.found: none. The only integrity checks in the component are the two artifact-stanza checksums, which cover config files, not images.

searched.for: the download-without-checksum asymmetry, to see whether it also affects these files
searched.found: nothing to report - both artifact stanzas carry options { checksum = "sha256:..." } and ledger-db has no artifact stanza. Stated because its absence would otherwise read as untested.

findings.title: The Go module declares an end-of-support language version and pins no toolchain
findings.class: CWE-1104 Use of Unmaintained Third Party Components
findings.evidence: `go 1.22` with no toolchain directive anywhere in the file. Go supports the two most recent major releases; the 1.22 series stopped receiving security fixes in early 2025.
findings.impact: This is the finding that a naive golang.org/x/net v0.22.0 CVE result was standing in front of. The gateway serves on stdlib net/http, and stdlib HTTP fixes - including the HTTP/2 CONTINUATION-flood fix that CVE-2023-45288 is usually cited for - ship in the toolchain, not in a module you can bump. With a go directive on an unsupported series and no toolchain line, nothing in the repository states which toolchain builds this, and a builder honouring the declared floor produces a binary carrying whatever stdlib bugs that series ended on. Low because in practice CI almost certainly runs a current Go and a current toolchain fixes it silently - but that is an assumption, and the repository is where it should have been written down.
findings.recommendation: Raise the go directive to a supported release and add an explicit toolchain line, so the build states the runtime it expects rather than inheriting whatever the builder happens to have.

triage.reason: The real control is the CI runner's Go version, which lives outside the repository. No CI configuration exists in the corpus to establish it, so this caps at probable - and 'CI probably runs something modern' is not HOLDS.

Bounded to low. The go directive is a language-version floor, not a toolchain pin: a modern toolchain builds this module and carries its own patched stdlib. The defect is that nothing records or enforces which one.
The sink is reachable - the gateway is a live net/http server, not a client-only or test-only use.

scope.established_by: Reading the go directive against Go's published support policy, then establishing that stdlib net/http is on a serving path via internal/gateway/http.go:9,142.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in-repo narrows it; the narrowing, if it exists, is the CI toolchain - which is exactly what is unrecorded.

searched.for: a toolchain directive or a godebug line that would pin or characterise the build runtime
searched.found: neither - the file is a bare module/go/require set

searched.looked_in: catalog-grpc-store/ for Dockerfile, .go-version, CI config, Makefile
searched.for: any other place the Go version is declared
searched.found: none of these files exist in the component; the go directive is the only statement of Go version anywhere
